intro: Albany Street splits in two just south of Prince Street and goes around a live oak. Brunswick built the road that way rather than move the tree, and local sources date Lover's Oak to the twelfth century, an age nobody has checked against a ring count. Ten heavy limbs branch low off a single trunk. A semi-truck took one of them off in 2015 and the tree carried on. It stands free and unfenced in the Old Town historic district, two blocks from the middle of downtown.

question_meta: Lover's Oak, a live oak the town dates to the twelfth century, stands in the middle of Albany Street in Brunswick's Old Town district. Free.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Brunswick is Lover's Oak, a southern live oak standing in the middle of Albany Street just south of Prince Street, in the Old Town historic district. The city dates it to the twelfth century, roughly nine hundred years, with no ring count or growth rate behind the figure, so read it as the age Brunswick has always used rather than a measurement. Ten main limbs branch low off a trunk cited at thirteen feet through, low enough to see how they carry their own weight. The street was laid around the tree instead of through it, which is the reason most people stop. It is free, unfenced and reachable at any hour.
question_context: Brunswick's Old Town historic district is a grid of streets and squares laid out in the eighteenth century, and Albany Street runs through the middle of it. The oak sits in the roadway just south of Prince Street with traffic passing on both sides, so park on a side street and walk the last block rather than trying to stop beside it. There is no fence, no fee and no gate; this is public street furniture in the most literal sense the phrase allows. Ten main limbs branch low from the trunk, which is what gives the tree its shape and what makes it worth standing under rather than driving past. One of the ten came off in 2015 when a semi-truck hit it, and the wound is part of what you see. Southern live oaks hold their leaves through winter and exchange them in spring, so no month is the wrong one. What coastal Georgia does have is a hard summer, which is an argument for going early in the day rather than for going in another season.

faq.a: Lover's Oak, a southern live oak in the middle of Albany Street just south of Prince Street. The city dates it to the twelfth century, about nine hundred years, though no ring count supports that figure.
Yes. It stands in a public street in the Old Town historic district, unfenced, with no ticket and no opening hours.

faq.q: How do I get there, and where do I park?
faq.a: It is two blocks from central downtown Brunswick, at Albany and Prince. Park on a side street and walk the last block; the tree is in the roadway, with traffic passing on both sides.

faq.q: When is the best time to see it?
faq.a: Any month. Live oaks are evergreen and swap their leaves in spring without going bare, so there is no season to catch. Early morning is the kinder hour in a coastal Georgia summer.

trees.story: Brunswick built its street around this oak instead of through it. Lover's Oak stands in the middle of Albany Street just south of Prince Street, ten main limbs branching low off one trunk, with the asphalt splitting and rejoining on either side of it. The city and Wikipedia both date it to the twelfth century, about nine hundred years, with no ring count or growth rate behind the number, so read that as the figure Brunswick has always used rather than anything measured. The trunk is cited at thirteen feet through, which is large enough for a live oak to be worth doubting; heavy buttressing at the base flatters a tape. What is not in doubt is what standing in a road costs. In 2015 a semi-truck hit the tree and tore off one of the ten limbs. It recovered, and traffic still goes around it. Southern live oaks are evergreen, swapping old leaves for new in spring without ever going bare, so there is no month to wait for and nothing to miss. It stands free and unfenced in the Old Town historic district, reachable at any hour, two blocks from the middle of downtown. The reason to walk those two blocks is not that it is the oldest thing in coastal Georgia. It is that a town rerouted itself around one tree and has never got round to changing its mind.
